steps.voiceover: The wizard lands on the Process step — the template gallery. It comes first on purpose, because it's the central decision. For the demo we pick a ready-made template, the Core SDLC flow. It gives us four agents that cover a full build-and-review loop: a Business Analyst who writes issues, a Developer who implements them, a Code Reviewer, and a Reworker. The live preview on the right confirms the hand-offs connect.
Next, the working environment — where the team operates. It bundles the repository, the branch, and the credentials into one reusable template, so we just pick one from the grid.
Step three gives the team its identity: a name and an ID, both pre-filled from the environment. The ID becomes the prefix for every agent the team creates, like agentic-demos-developer.
Knowledge is optional. Here we choose the skills every member inherits, the sources it can query at runtime, and how learnings are shared across the team. We accept the defaults.
Finally, review — everything in one place. When we hit create, the wizard builds the whole team in one atomic transaction, each member with its own chat identity, ready for the first issue.

The most intuitive kind is a scheduled trigger. I pick Cron, choose Daily at 07:00 — the platform confirms it in plain language and shows the cron expression — and write the prompt the agent runs every morning, unattended.
The simplest type is Once — a one-shot that fires a single time at a moment you pick, then removes itself. Here it delivers a personal reminder.

An HTTP webhook lets an external system fire the trigger. The panel generates a dedicated endpoint and a required secret — copy it once into your calling system; there's no open, unauthenticated mode.

This is the type doing the real work in a flow. I pick the repository and one event from the full catalog — here Issue labeled — and narrow it to a single label, "ready", so the agent reacts to precisely the signal it cares about.

The subtlest type is a data-flow dependency. It reframes a push as a hand-off between teammates: an upstream agent committed its work, so now it's your turn. The woken agent pulls, checks relevance, and continues — or replies PASS.
A draft is an editable process that exists before any team is created — nothing is live, nothing spawned. Here's a fresh, empty one called Simple SDLC. Let's add our first agent.
I click Add agent and choose "From scratch". Instead of writing a system prompt by hand, I give the agent a name and jot down one line of intent: take requirements and create a GitHub issue.

Here's where we are: two agents on the canvas, each with its generated prompt — but standing side by side, unconnected. Two agents that don't hand work to each other aren't a process yet. The next step makes it a flow.

I drag from the Business Analyst's port onto the Developer and choose an Issue channel: the BA opens an issue that wakes the Developer. I add a routing label, "ready", and tick the human approval gate — so the Developer only starts once a person applies that label. And there it is: a working, human-gated flow.

As a final touch I turn on Stages, and the flow organises into labelled bands — Requirements holding the BA, Build holding the Developer. From here, one click on Materialize would turn this drawing into a live, running team. That's the whole story of Flows: design it visually, and go live only when you're ready.
